While searching for a tonkatsu restaurant on the Internet, I came across Katsu Restaurant and decided to visit it.

The sirloin cutlet I saw on the internet wasn't the type I expected from high-end tonkatsu restaurants with the fat attached to one end, but they said they used first-grade pork and it seemed to have a good feel, so I was curious.

Naver Map showed it as if it was in a back alley like the last time I guided Jongno Hammubara, but when I got off the bus and looked at the main street before going to the back alley, it was on the main road. I almost wasted my efforts going down the back alleys just by looking at the Naver map.

It was around 12 o'clock, and the interior of the relatively Japanese-style restaurant was filled with many customers who seemed to be office workers. I was sitting at a table for two by the window, wondering whether to order sirloin katsu or tenderloin katsu, which looked better. I asked the older male owner, who brought me cold water in a bottle, whether sirloin katsu comes with fat attached to one end. I thought it would be less attractive if it wasn't soft, so I ordered the tenderloin cutlet, which was said to be moist and soft.

Customers kept coming in, and by the time the tenderloin cutlet I ordered was served, all the seats were occupied.

When I looked at the tenderloin cutlet, there were three small, round pieces of tenderloin cutlet cut in half, making a total of six pieces, and it consisted of rice, cabbage salad, miso soup, radish radish and pickled radish, dried red pepper, tonkatsu sauce, and wasabi.

First, I put the salt prepared on the table on top of a juicy piece of tenderloin cutlet and tasted it. It was chewy and juicy and had no unpleasant smell and had a good flavor. The meat juice is dripping from the bottom of the tenderloin cutlet I just ate.

Next, I topped it with wasabi and dipped it in tonkatsu sauce and tasted it. The tonkatsu sauce had an apple-flavored sweetness and could be refreshing, but I didn't like the tonkatsu sauce having this kind of scent.

This time I picked up the cabbage salad and tasted it. The sesame dressing was nutty and the salad was moist and plentiful.

The miso soup wasn't the type you get at a high-end tonkatsu restaurant, but tasted like something you'd find at a regular tonkatsu restaurant.

The pickled radish and chili peppers that came as side dishes were ordinary, and the radish radish radish was soft but had a slightly sour taste, which was less good.

Overall, this is a store where you can enjoy tonkatsu, which is somewhere between high-end tonkatsu and regular tonkatsu, at a relatively low price. It's worth stopping by when you're nearby.

reviews.text:
After seeing my favorite singer busking on the street in Hongdae, I walked to the end of Yeontral Park and arrived at an okonomiyaki restaurant. Because it is near Sacheon Bridge, it is located in a relatively quiet commercial district compared to Yeonnam-dong.

Nevertheless, as it is currently one of the hottest Japanese restaurants in Hongdae, there was a wait even though it was aimed at an ambiguous time slot on a weekday. To begin with, the size of the store is quite small, so there is not a lot of capacity.

Fortunately, there was a lot to see around and there was a famous curry bakery next door, so I made the most of my time and entered. We were guided to a two-person room in a renovated warehouse-like space, and although it seemed small, it was more comfortable than expected.

However, I couldn't shake off the feeling of awkwardness as I sat alone with the two men, especially my older brother, who was a junior in the military. It was a completely separate room from the entrance, but there was only a small hole in the wall leading to the hall and kitchen.

As a side dish, pickled onions with a refreshing yet sweet taste are provided, and kimchi is provided upon request. For okonomiyaki, I tried both Hiroshima and Osaka styles, so after a long time of deliberation, I ordered Osaka style.

In Japan, it is common to eat one plate per person, but the owner said that one plate was enough for two people, so I added just one bowl of yakisoba. Draft beer was a must, and the foamy foam was impressive.

Sauces such as teriyaki and mayonnaise are provided at the table, and the teriyaki was a product I saw at the Hiroshima Hassho. The owner recommended that I eat okonomiyaki with some teriyaki as a side dish.

The okonomiyaki was very generous as it filled the entire plate, and was different from the Hiroshima style of stacking layers one after another. The dough and ingredients were all mixed together, so in a way it had an esoteric Osaka style.

There were a few ingredients that were not found in the traditional okonomiyaki style, such as dried rice cakes, nuts, and chips, which felt like a slight variation. It is in the same context that the fried egg that I requested was half-boiled.

When I took a beautiful piece and tasted it, the overall lightness was evident, and the rich texture and taste of Osaka-style ingredients and batter came together. The chips were spicy, adding a stimulating kick and fun.

Although it was Osaka-style okonomiya with a low point, the solid basics stood out with a good arrangement of the taste and texture of ingredients such as vegetables, seafood, nuts, and chips. I also liked the feeling that the space for the mayonnaise was left blank on purpose.

Next, contrary to expectations, the Yakisoba had a thick and sticky sauce and a lot of sweetness. It had a sweet-salty center, so it felt like you were bitten right away, and above all, it didn't go well with okonomiyaki.

Perhaps because I expected a salty and dry style, it seemed a bit burdensome at first impression. Fortunately, the spiciness was somewhat balanced by the inclusion of finely chopped green onions.

Anyway, the okonomiyaki was okay and the variation factor was a lot of fun. Even though I compared it to Japan, I felt that the style was quite different, and in terms of friendliness, it ranked first among the restaurants I went to this year.

The soup you first encounter is clear and hearty enough to be called a warm version of Pyongyang naengmyeon. However, as it boils, the sweetness of the vegetables and the meat broth combine to create a deep umami flavor. Today, Park Tung's pick is Manna Restaurant in nearby Seongsan-dong.
I entered with a bit of embarrassment as the interior was smaller than expected (there are 10 people in total, including 2 tables). The table spacing is narrow and the table size is small.
I tried to sit where I wanted to sit, but they cheerfully offered me another seat, so I took a different seat.
Kimchi was served as geotjeori, and the radish radish kimchi and seasoned bean sprouts that came with it suited my tastes and made me slightly excited about the food.
They told me I could eat the dumplings once they started boiling, so I grabbed one, but the warmth didn't reach the center, but I remembered that hotpot is made with dumplings that have been steamed anyway, so I just ate it.
Perhaps they boil the cabbage and clams together when making the basic soup, but the cabbage was well cooked and the clams looked quite chewy, but I couldn't taste the unique taste of clams.
After eating it all, I feel like I ate quite healthy food. It has a mild taste, but it has a spicy feel because it contains pepper. However, I left out the cooked peppers because they had a bit of a tough texture.
The food is delicious, and although it's a small space where you can eat shoulder-to-shoulder, I would visit again.

Hippo Brunch House is already famous as a brunch restaurant in Yeonnam-dong, and when I went there in person, I immediately understood why so many people visit it. Even though I visited in the morning, there were quite a lot of customers and I saw many foreigners, so I felt like I was on a trip.

The store is larger than expected, with dining available on both the first and basement floors, and there are plenty of seating options. The overall atmosphere was bright and stylish, so I didn't feel pressured to stay for a long time, and it was nice to enjoy brunch while chatting. It would be great to eat outside especially when the weather gets warm because there is terrace seating.

The menu items I ordered were truffle cream soup, ragout pasta, all the wave brunch, and orange mango juice, and I was satisfied with all of them. The truffle cream soup has a strong scent that makes you feel good from the first spoonful, and it is smooth, so it was the perfect start to brunch. The sauce for the ragouta pasta was so rich that I was impressed as soon as I took a bite! It's a great brunch restaurant, and I was surprised by the high quality of the pasta. All the Wave Lunch was well-organized and the plating was pretty, so it was fun to try a variety of things.
Even if it's not necessarily brunch, it's a great place to have a cup of coffee or a drink.

I think I can confidently recommend this place when making a brunch appointment in Yeonnam-dong because it is a place with a high level of overall satisfaction from the atmosphere, taste, and menu composition. Next time, I want to come back to the terrace on a nice day ☀️

reviews.author: ethan ghymn
reviews.text:
I like Japanese curry, so I make it a point to visit a curry restaurant on a regular basis, but after seeing this restaurant in Masdoedin's review, I saved it as a place I wanted to go.

On the way to Hongdae to have dinner, I called in advance to inquire if there was any curry bread sold out at a popular store, and they said they fried the most curry bread today and that they had all kinds, so I decided to stop by first before dinner.

The store was located inside the neighborhood, and when I looked at it on Naver Maps, it used to be a repair shop called Best Reform House, but the exterior had been kept the same as before, giving off a retro feel. When I entered the store, it seemed like they had four different types of curry bread on display on one side of the small store and also sold lemonade.

I couldn't eat them all before dinner, so I asked them to pack one basic meat curry bread and one spicy curry bread for me. They asked if they wanted to eat it right away. When I told them that they wanted to eat the meat curry bread right away, they told me that the meat curry bread was most recently fried and handed it to me in a paper bag while informing me that it was labeled by type.

A woman who appeared to be frying curry bread in the kitchen behind the counter, hidden by a curtain, peeked out her head for a moment as if wondering which customer had come to buy it, then disappeared behind the curtain again.

After standing on the side of the street and checking the type on the bottom of the package, I took out the basic meat curry bread and tasted it. It was not the wide round type, but rather a small, round and elongated type. It looked somewhat like a glutinous rice donut covered in sugar. However, the bread crumbs on the outside were not the fine and lightly crispy type, but the volume was a bit disappointing than expected, so I hope the taste is good.

When I take a bite, it smells like Indian curry, so the curry is good, but the temperature is lukewarm and the bread crumbs on the outside are not lightly crispy like tonkatsu, and the texture of the bread would be nice if it were a little lighter and airier, but it wasn't, and it was a bit disappointing that it felt a little sticky on the back.

When I got home, I tried the spicy curry bread and it was good because it wasn't too spicy and just a little more spicy.

I like Japanese curry overall, so I stopped by a store that specializes in curry bread. In Japan, I think you can probably taste good enough curry bread for around 150 to 200 yen, but considering that the basic meat curry bread costs 3,600 won, and the volume and texture of the bread are a bit disappointing, I feel like it's okay, but considering that even crappy donuts are sold well in the 3,000-5,000 won range in Korea, I understand it and don't bother. I don't know if I'll visit again, but since it's a rare store, I hope it gets better and it's delicious.
